documents.title: Artificial Intelligence in Education
documents.summary: An academic-integrity office hub that frames GenAI as a disruption to teaching and assessment and promotes AI literacy through a Canvas module, workshops and guides. It sets no campus-wide rule on student AI use and hands course policy to instructors, supporting them with resources.
documents.stance_why: The page never says AI is banned or allowed; it says 'Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change', offers an AI literacy module so instructors can 'guide students in using GenAI tools ethically and responsibly for your course(s)', and links to a guide for 'Crafting Your GenAI Course Policy'. The decision stays with instructors, so the stance is delegates.

units.why: Says 'Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change' because of LLMs. It calls for assessment redesign in general terms, so it fits P35 only partly: no specific redesign is given. Informs, addressed to all.
units.anchor: Teaching, learning and assessments all need to change.
units.fit_note: General claim that assessment must change; no specific redesign is named.

units.why: States the page will 'keep the UC San Diego community up-to-date', a commitment to ongoing updating of guidance. It is closest to P54 (policy revisited) but it is a page of updates, not a policy review cycle.
units.anchor: This page will try to keep the UC San Diego community up-to-date
units.fit_note: Commitment to keep a guidance page current, not a formal review of a policy.

units.why: Says GenAI tools 'can replace and augment human thinking' and 'hinder and accelerate learning', naming both benefits and risks. It states benefits, so P87, but it is balanced rather than only positive.
units.anchor: GenAI tools present both challenges and opportunities for education.

units.why: Cites survey results that students are worried about critical thinking and that '47% believe its easier to cheat with the tools'. This is data about AI's effect on students, so P55 (evidence), informs.
units.anchor: 47% believe its easier to cheat with the tools
units.fit_note: Survey of student attitudes rather than learning outcomes.

units.why: 'Although there is not yet campus-sponsored AI Literacy training, you can help educate students.' Encourages instructors to provide AI literacy education, so P70 (training), addressed to instructors with 'can' read as should.
units.anchor: there is not yet campus-sponsored AI Literacy training, you can help educate students
units.fit_note: Notes campus lacks training and asks instructors to fill the gap.

units.why: Warns that instructors 'may falsely believe that so-called "AI detectors" are valid and accurate'. This tells instructors detectors are not reliable, so P39.
units.anchor: Instructors may falsely believe that so-called "AI detectors" are valid and accurate

units.why: 'Students accept Grammarly suggestions without realizing that they are AI generated' points to AI embedded in everyday tools. It is awareness of embedded AI, so P07 only partly: no rule is set.
units.anchor: Students accept Grammarly suggestions without realizing that they are AI generated
units.fit_note: Describes embedded AI that students may not notice; sets no rule.

units.why: Defines 'AI literacy is the ability to identify if, when, where, and why to use GenAI tools', a definition that sets the scope of the literacy effort. P61, informs.
units.anchor: AI literacy is the ability to identify if, when, where, and why to use GenAI

units.why: Lists 'Critical evaluation of AI-generated content: Assessing AI outputs, understanding their origins, potential biases, and limitations' as a key aspect of AI literacy. It asks users to evaluate AI output, so P31.
units.anchor: Critical evaluation of AI-generated content: Assessing AI outputs, understanding their origins
units.fit_note: Framed as a literacy competency, not a duty to verify submitted work.

units.why: 'Ethical reasoning and risk awareness' includes 'privacy, fairness, and accountability' and 'algorithmic bias'. It names ethical and bias concerns as part of literacy, so P53.
units.anchor: Exploring moral implications of AI use, including privacy, fairness, and accountability

units.why: 'Adaptation and continuous learning: Staying informed about AI advancements' is a listed aspect of literacy that asks users to keep up with AI developments, so P102.
units.anchor: Staying informed about AI advancements and developing skills to adapt to evolving AI technologies.

units.why: 'AI literacy is not about promoting AI use' states the purpose of the literacy effort and its limit. No type says this directly (P56 is a framework, P44 the opposite), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: AI literacy is not about promoting AI use.
units.uncovered_note: AI literacy education is explicitly not meant to promote AI use but to build critical thinking and recognise where human judgment is irreplaceable.

units.why: The Canvas module is 'a resource to support instructors to introduce students to fundamental AI competencies', i.e. an institution-provided AI literacy module for students. P70.
units.anchor: a resource to support instructors to introduce students to fundamental AI competencies

units.why: 'Create a Q&A discussion forum to encourage ongoing dialogue' asks instructors to discuss AI with students beyond listing rules, so P66 (explain and discuss), should.
units.anchor: Create a Q&A discussion forum to encourage ongoing dialogue

units.why: Offers 'a GenAI in Education Presentation, Workshop, or Consultation' with the director, which is faculty support for learning about AI, so P63.
units.anchor: Request a GenAI in Education Presentation

units.why: 'Engaged Teaching Hubs AI Literacy for Faculty Coffee Chats' is a faculty community offering on AI, so P63.
units.anchor: Engaged Teaching Hubs AI Literacy for Faculty Coffee Chats

units.why: Lists 'The Library's GenAI and Academic Integrity Guide' among student resources, pointing students to library help beyond AI tools. P72 fits only partly because it is a listed link, not a directive.
units.anchor: The Library's GenAI and Academic Integrity Guide
units.fit_note: A resource link; no instruction to seek human help.

units.why: Quotes Dobrin that students 'need to be taught how to use these tools responsibly, effectively, and efficiently', a professional-skill argument for teaching AI use. P44.
units.anchor: They need to be taught how to use these tools responsibly, effectively, and efficiently

documents.title: Top 10 Tips for Instructors
documents.summary: Ten tips for instructors on upholding academic integrity, with several that address AI: state expectations, redesign assessments, report suspected violations. It gives a sample syllabus sentence but leaves the AI rule itself to each instructor.
documents.stance_why: The tips tell instructors to 'be exceptionally clear' about AI and to craft their own 'GenAI & AI Policy', and offer sample wording; the page sets no university-wide permission or ban. Decision rests with instructors, so delegates.

units.why: 'Creating a class Statement of Values ... with your students is key' asks instructors to build integrity expectations together with students for buy-in, so P67.
units.anchor: with your students is key.

units.why: The class statement 'must be aligned (and certainly not contradict) the university's Academic Integrity Policy' ties course rules to existing university policy, so P77.
units.anchor: must be aligned (and certainly not contradict) the university's

units.why: 'if you will not allow "open-notes" exams no matter what, state that up front and why' asks instructors to give reasons linked to learning, so P66.
units.anchor: state that up front and why - make sure to connect it to learning

units.why: 'everyone is accountable for reporting violations of the code or values' makes students and staff responsible for reporting breaches of the class code. Closest is P81 (reporting procedure), partly.
units.anchor: everyone is accountable for reporting violations of the code or values
units.fit_note: Duty to report breaches of a class code, not a formal central report.

units.why: 'Ensure that the learning objectives for the course are clearly stated, and each activity... connected back to those learning objectives' ties assessment to learning objectives to reduce cheating. P83 fits partly since it is not about AI decisions specifically.
units.anchor: Ensure that the learning objectives for the course are clearly stated
units.fit_note: Presented as a mastery-orientation tip, not tied to AI permission.

units.why: 'Provide multiple attempts at several low/no-stakes assessments' is an instructor action to ease grade pressure that drives cheating, so P99.
units.anchor: Provide multiple attempts at several low/ no-stakes assessments (formative) before the summative assessments

units.why: 'Given the advancements in artificial intelligence, be exceptionally clear!' tells instructors to state their expectations on AI use, matching P09 (state AI expectations).
units.anchor: Given the advancements in artificial intelligence, be exceptionally clear!

units.why: Sample sentence: 'Open books/notes does not mean that you can get ... artificial intelligence to answer the exam questions for you.' It bars AI on exams even when notes are open, so P22.
units.anchor: artificial intelligence to answer the exam questions for you.

units.why: Sample sentence: 'Stay away from sites and tools (e.g., Chegg, Coursehero, ChatGPT, CoPilot) that will do your work for you'. Students may not have tools do the work they submit, so P19.
units.anchor: Stay away from sites and tools (e.g., Chegg, Coursehero, ChatGPT, CoPilot)

units.why: The sample text says such actions 'result in an academic integrity violation and a report to the Academic Integrity Office', classifying misuse as misconduct, so P36.
units.anchor: result in an academic integrity violation and a report to the Academic Integrity Office

units.why: 'If you're not sure about which tools are appropriate for you to use, ask!' tells students to ask when unsure, so P10.
units.anchor: If you're not sure about which tools are appropriate for you to use, ask!

units.why: 'If you haven't yet crafted your GenAI & AI Policy, you can find guidance, examples, and templates here' offers support to instructors setting their own policy and implies each writes one. Best fit P63 (support), and P04 does not fit because it is not stated as a rule.
units.anchor: If you haven't yet crafted your GenAI & AI Policy, you can find
units.fit_note: Also assumes instructors write their own AI policy.

units.why: 'Consider alternative assessment methods' because earlier assessments 'may no longer be the right assessments'. Asks for assessment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Consider alternative assessment methods.

units.why: 'rethink your learning objectives by considering which ones are easy ... to cognitively offload to artificial intelligence' makes AI decisions follow from learning objectives, so P83.
units.anchor: rethink your learning objectives by considering

units.why: 'Break your assessments into parts, i.e., scaffold them' because AI is poor at scaffolding across assignments. A redesign of assignments around AI, P35.
units.anchor: Break your assessments into parts, i.e., scaffold them.

units.why: 'Create a scaffolded assignment where the students use AI tools' suggests building AI use into an assignment, so P79.
units.anchor: Create a scaffolded assignment where the students use AI tools
units.fit_note: Offered as an idea, not a requirement.

units.why: 'Consider using Oral Assessments' is a way to check understanding by having students explain, so P34.
units.anchor: Consider using Oral Assessments

units.why: 'Teach students how to do something without AI, and then once they've mastered that, allow them to cognitively offload that skill to AI' stages AI permission as skill develops, P08.
units.anchor: Teach students how to do something without AI, and then once they’ve mastered

units.why: 'Flip your classroom! Have students ... come into class to do activities and demonstrate knowledge and skills' moves evaluation into class. P33 fits partly since it does not say weight shifts to proctored work.
units.anchor: Flip your classroom!
units.fit_note: In-class demonstration of skill, not stated as proctored grading.

units.why: Instructors who 'require the use of any artificial intelligence tools' must think about 'privacy', 'security' and 'equity (do all students have access?)'. Equity of access is P51; it also covers privacy so fit is partial.
units.anchor: equity (do all students have access?) issues if you decide to remote proctor
units.fit_note: Also raises privacy and security of required AI tools and remote proctoring.

units.why: 'have students reaffirm their commitment to that statement or code on each assessment' uses timely integrity reminders to cut cheating, i.e. reducing misuse pressure, P99 (closest; not a response to misuse).
units.anchor: have students reaffirm their commitment to that statement or code on each assessment
units.fit_note: Prevention by reminder of integrity rather than easing pressure.

units.why: 'check in on your students' activities' and reach out to those struggling 'can mitigate any temptations ... to use outside services or unpermitted aids'. Easing the causes of misuse, P99.
units.anchor: reach out to students individually and/or survey the class as a whole

units.why: 'Follow-up with each student to talk through at least one of their answers' checks understanding before grading, a form of explain-your-work check, P34.
units.anchor: Follow-up with each student to talk through at least one of their answers.

units.why: 'Use Turnitin in Canvas for any narrative exams and check all assignments' tells instructors to use similarity software to find misuse, P40.
units.anchor: Use Turnitin in Canvas for any narrative exams and check all assignments

units.why: 'use their metrics and logs to check for signs of integrity violations' and 'horizontal grading' use activity logs and grading practice to identify misuse, P40.
units.anchor: use their metrics and logs to check for signs of integrity violations

units.why: 'The Academic Senate Academic Integrity Policy requires all instructors to report all suspected integrity violations' sets a mandatory reporting duty (formal report form), P81.
units.anchor: requires all i instructors to report all suspected integrity violations.

units.why: 'submit an Intent to Report, which restricts the student(s) from making changes to the class' is a procedural step while investigating, P81.
units.anchor: Intent to Report

units.why: Responding to violations leverages 'the teachable moment for students', an educative framing of misuse, P68.
units.anchor: leverage the teachable moment for students
units.fit_note: Used as a reason to report violations, not to choose a remedial response.

units.why: 'Any extenuating circumstances ... will be considered during the sanctioning phase' says context shapes sanctions. No type covers this exactly, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Any extenuating circumstances that led to the integrity violations will be considered
units.uncovered_note: Extenuating circumstances are considered when sanctions are decided for integrity violations.

units.why: 'If you reported cheating last year, share that information with your class this year' is deterrence by telling students violations are reported. It fits no type (P66 is reasons for AI rules), so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: If you reported cheating last year, share that information with your class
units.uncovered_note: Instructors tell students that past violations were reported, to deter cheating.

units.why: Tip 10 offers 'Pedagogical/ Assessment/ Culture Consultations' and presentations from the Academic Integrity Office, which is support for faculty on AI and integrity, P63.
units.anchor: Reach Out to AIO for Assistance

notes: Only two university-level Academic Integrity Office pages were screened in; no school or computing policy found. Navigation text and link lists were skipped. Several fit_notes mark integrity-prevention tips (P99) and a deterrence-by-reporting tip that no type covers well.
